title: Inventory, overselling and flash sales
subtitle: Sell the last item exactly once, even when thousands of people tap "Buy" in the same second, and tell them the truth while they wait.

c.v: A shop in Bengaluru runs a midnight sale: 500 pairs of a limited sneaker at ₹4,999. Marketing has been posting about it for two weeks.
At 00:00, about 40,000 people tap "Buy" within the first minute. The checkout code reads the stock, checks that it is above zero, and then writes the new number.

The sale page says "sold out" after 90 seconds. Everyone celebrates. The next morning, the warehouse counts 523 paid orders for 500 pairs. Twenty-three customers get a refund and an apology email. Several post screenshots online.
There was a second problem. During the first minute, checkout pages took 20 seconds to load. The stock row was the bottleneck. Every purchase had to wait its turn for that one row.
happens when two requests check the stock at the same time. Both see "1 left". Both decide to sell. Both write. This is a race between a read and a write. It is the same bug as the
The fix is simple: do not check in your app code. Ask the database to check and change the number in one step. If the number is already zero, the database changes nothing, and you show "sold out".

that keeps you correct also makes buyers wait one at a time. So you also need ways to spread the work, and to let fewer people in at once.

Correct stock is a single number that only the database may change, in one atomic step. Speed comes from splitting that number, and from controlling who reaches checkout. It never comes from skipping the check.

Keep these transactions short. Never call a payment API while you hold the lock. If you lock more than one row, always lock them in the same order, such as by ID. Postgres advises this to avoid

You can hold stock when the buyer starts checkout, not only at payment time. Shopify's inventory model has states for held stock. It splits the units on hand into states such as available, committed and reserved.
is a row like "1 unit for cart 88, until 00:10". Your

moves one unit from available to reserved. Payment turns the reservation into a sale. A small job, or a check at read time, releases reservations that expire. Without expiry, people who leave without paying keep stock held forever.
Pick the expiry from real data, like how long most people take to pay. A short expiry frees stock fast. Too short, and buyers lose the item while typing a card number.
In a flash sale, every buyer updates the same row. A transaction holds the row lock until it commits. So, as Alibaba's PolarDB docs explain, updates to one
run one at a time. The docs say
the database or tables gives limited gains here.
Alibaba calls this the "inventory hotspot" problem. A researcher from its database team says it solved the problem in time for Double Eleven in 2013.
You cannot remove this waiting, but you can make each turn shorter. Do only the stock UPDATE inside the transaction. Do the rest of the order, like the address and the email, outside it.

This section is our advice, not a method from the sources above. Split one stock number into several rows. For example, store 500 sneakers as 10 bucket rows of 50. Each request picks a bucket at random and runs the conditional UPDATE on it. Now 10 purchases can run at the same time, not one.

When a bucket is empty, try another. Near the end, a buyer may see "sold out" while one other bucket still has a pair. You can handle this with a final pass over all buckets, or a small job that moves leftover units. In Postgres,
skips rows that others hold. The docs say it gives an inconsistent view, but it suits queue-like tables.
That makes it useful to pick any free bucket.
Even a fast database has a limit. So control how many people reach checkout. Shopify learned this in its flash sales. Checkout writes were taking down parts of the platform.
It added a throttle, a limit on how many buyers get through, in its
. Buyers over the limit saw a cached queue page that checked again from time to time.
The first version picked people at random. Some customers waited up to 40 minutes for a sale that lasted 40 minutes.
The fix stored each buyer's first attempt time in a signed cookie, so earlier buyers would not lose out to later ones.
You can also buy this as a product. Cloudflare's
admits visitors based on two limits: total active users and new users per minute. Others wait in a first-in-first-out queue and see an estimated wait time.
The product page might get 100 times more views than purchases. Do not hit the stock row for each view.

But the cache is only a hint. The conditional UPDATE at checkout is the truth. A stale cache may show "in stock" for a few seconds after the last sale. That is fine, as long as checkout says "sold out" clearly.

Tell people where they stand. Show their place in the queue or an estimated wait. When stock runs out, tell everyone in the queue at once, so they stop waiting. When a buyer reaches checkout, say how long their item is held. If you ever do oversell, refund fast and say sorry plainly.

c.v: Search the code for "read stock, then write stock". Replace each case with a conditional UPDATE, and check the rows-changed count.
Ask product: "How long do we hold an item in checkout? What do we tell a buyer when it expires?"
Before a big sale, load-test checkout for the one hot product, not a spread of products. See
Add a check that runs every few minutes: units sold plus units available must equal the starting stock. Alert if they differ.
Plan for the user, not just the database: a queue page, a clear "sold out" for everyone, and a refund plan.
Keep the stock transaction tiny. No payment calls, emails or HTTP calls while a row lock is held.
"Find every place in this repo where we read stock and then update it in separate statements. Rewrite each one as a single conditional UPDATE, and handle 0 rows as sold out."
"Write a test that starts 50 parallel purchases against a product with stock 10, using a real Postgres database. Assert that exactly 10 succeed and stock ends at 0."
"Design a stock-bucket scheme for one product with 500 units in 10 rows. Show how a buyer picks a bucket, and what happens when the chosen bucket is empty."
The test really runs purchases in parallel, against a real database. A loop that buys one at a time proves nothing.
The code checks the rows-changed count. An UPDATE that changes 0 rows does not raise an error.
No network call happens inside the stock transaction.
Expired reservations go back to available stock, and this has its own test.

q.v: Your code reads stock, checks it is above 0 in the app, then writes stock − 1. What happens when two buyers try for the last item at once?

options.v: The database stops the second buyer automatically.
Both can read 1, both write 0, and you sell two items you do not have.
The second write fails with an error.

why.v: The check and the write are separate steps. Both requests pass the check before either one writes.

q.v: In Postgres (Read Committed), two requests run UPDATE items SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 7 AND stock > 0 when stock is 1. What happens?

options.v: One changes 1 row. The other waits, checks the WHERE again on the new value, and changes 0 rows.

why.v: Postgres makes the second updater wait, then re-checks the WHERE clause on the updated row. 0 rows changed means sold out.

q.v: A flash sale has 1,000 units of one product in one row. Checkout is slow even though the database CPU is low. What is the likely cause?

options.v: Every purchase waits for the lock on the same hot row, so updates run one at a time.

why.v: Updates to one row are serialized by its lock. Splitting stock into several bucket rows lets purchases run in parallel.

q.v: Why put a time limit on a stock reservation?

options.v: So stock held by people who leave without paying goes back on sale.

why.v: Without expiry, abandoned checkouts keep items held forever, and the site shows sold out while the shelf is full.
